Reading the transmittance check. Averaged over leaves, the reflectance fit has RMSE 0.0082 with 91% in-sample predictive coverage. The held-out transmittance prediction has RMSE 0.0526 and only 27% coverage. The T errors are smooth and systematic rather than noisy: they are model-structure and parameter errors, not measurement noise. That is exactly what the iid model’s single σ cannot describe. It also matches the known weakness of reflectance-only PROSPECT inversion: N, Cw and Cm trade off against each other, and R alone cannot pin down how light is split between transmittance and absorptance. Practical consequences:

Fitting R and T jointly is much better when T exists. The forward model already returns both in every backend, so this only changes the likelihood.
When only R is available, the posterior must be widened honestly. That is the job of the structured error models on the Error models page, which this check can then evaluate.

title: Methods
text:
Forward model: PROSPECT-D
PROSPECT treats a leaf as a stack of \(N\) absorbing plates. For each wavelength \(\lambda\), the absorption coefficient of one elementary layer is
\[
k(\lambda) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_j C_j\, K_j(\lambda),
\]
where \(C_j\) are constituent contents and \(K_j\) their specific absorption coefficients. For PROSPECT-D, \(j \in\) {chlorophyll \(C_{ab}\), carotenoids \(C_{ar}\), anthocyanins \(C_{anth}\), brown pigments \(C_{brown}\), water \(C_w\), dry matter \(C_m\)} (Féret et al. 2017).
The transmissivity of a compact layer is
\[
\tau(k) = (1-k)\,e^{-k} + k^2 E_1(k),
\qquad E_1(x) = \int_x^\infty \frac{e^{-t}}{t}\,dt .
\]
Reflectance and transmittance then follow from Allen et al. (1969) for a single plate, with interface transmissivities \(t_{\alpha}=\bar t(40^\circ, n)\), \(t_{12}=\bar t(90^\circ, n)\) and \(t_{21}=t_{12}/n^2\) (Stern 1964). Stokes’ (1862) solution then gives \(N\) plates. The three \(\bar t\) vectors depend only on the refractive index, so they are precomputed once in scripts/prepare_data.py.
Versions. Every implementation takes a coefficient matrix \(K\) (wavelength × constituent) and a constituent vector \(C\), so a PROSPECT version is just data. config/models.json defines PROSPECT-D, 5B, 5 and 4. The coefficient tables are in data/coefficients/. Adding PROSPECT-PRO (protein and carbon-based constituents) means adding its coefficient table and a JSON entry; no backend code changes.

The exponential integral \(E_1\)
None of Stan, NIMBLE or PyTensor ships an \(E_1\), so each backend has two modes.

exact (default): a library implementation, with the analytic derivative \(\frac{d}{dx}E_1(x) = -e^{-x}/x\) supplied explicitly wherever gradients are needed. The special function itself is therefore never differentiated.
approx: the Swamee & Ohija (2003) closed form \(E_1(x) \approx \left(A^{-7.7} + B\right)^{-0.13}\), with \(A=\ln\!\big((0.56146/x+0.65)(1+x)\big)\) and \(B=x^4 e^{7.7x}(2+x)^{3.7}\). It is cheap and differentiable in any DSL. See Forward model for its error.

E₁ is about a quarter of the Numba gradient cost. The fast E₁ cuts E₁ from 204 to 88 µs. The full log-density + gradient drops from 669 to 530 µs.
JAX’s built-in exp1 is very slow on CPU: 6,075 µs for 2101 values, about 30× Cephes. It evaluates a fixed number of series and continued-fraction iterations for every element. Swapping in the fast E₁ makes the JAX gradient 8× faster.
Swamee–Ohija is the slowest option in both frameworks. Its value is cheap to compute, but automatic differentiation through its log/pow/exp chain costs more than the exact function with an analytic gradient. Stan showed the same effect (Backends).
With the fast E₁, the remaining cost is the rest of PROSPECT (exp, pow, sqrt and about ten divisions per band). Fusing everything into one hand-written Numba loop does not help: 2101 bands fit in cache, so the cost is arithmetic, not memory traffic.

With the exact or fast \(E_1\), every sampler matches Stan to within 0.13 posterior SDs: Monte Carlo error. With Swamee–Ohija the largest shift is 0.60 SDs, mostly in σ. That is not sampling error: the approximation changes the model slightly, by the same amount for every sampler and in Stan (Backends). NoteA pitfall found along the way: get_jaxified_logp(negative_logp=False)





Despite its name, pymc.sampling.jax.get_jaxified_logp(model, negative_logp=False) returns the potential \(-\log p\). This is what PyMC passes to NumPyro as potential_fn. Wrapping it as potential_fn=lambda x: -logp(x), which the name invites, makes NumPyro target \(1/p\), an improper density. Nothing errors, and the draws look like a plausible but wrong posterior. The first version of python/fit_pymc.py had this bug. It was caught because σ disagreed with the five reference backends.









NoteTwo Numba pitfalls when giving a PyTensor Op its own kernel






Error model. Numba’s default error_model="python" raises a Python ZeroDivisionError on float division by zero. A NUTS trajectory that briefly reaches \(k \to 0\) or \(\infty\) then crashes the whole fit instead of being rejected. One pm.sample fit did exactly that. The kernels now use error_model="numpy" (inf/NaN, which the sampler rejects) and no fastmath, which would let LLVM assume every input is finite.
Stale cache. PyTensor caches compiled Numba kernels on disk, keyed by the Op’s type and properties but not its code. Editing a kernel therefore silently keeps the old one until the cache key is salted. The kernels return (fn, version) from register_funcify_default_op_cache_key. Every fast-E₁ fit that used Numba was re-run after this fix.

title: Faster PyMC: samplers × E₁
text:
Would a GPU (JAX) help?
This section is reasoning, not measurement: no GPU was available.
For one spectrum: probably a small gain, or none.

Each gradient is tiny. It is a few hundred thousand floating-point operations on 2101 numbers, and NUTS needs each gradient before it can take the next step. A GPU would be limited by the fixed cost of launching work (about 5–10 µs per kernel), not by compute.

With NumPyro or BlackJAX, the whole NUTS loop is compiled and stays on the GPU, so there is no copying back and forth.
Each gradient might then take tens of µs, against 530 µs on one CPU core here.

But PROSPECT needs float64. The Stokes step subtracts nearly equal numbers (\(v_b^{2(N-1)} - 1\)), so float32 is risky for thick leaves. Consumer GPUs run float64 at 1/32 to 1/64 of their float32 speed. On an A100 or H100 a single leaf might run a few times faster; on a gaming card, probably no faster.
The E₁ problem gets worse. JAX’s exp1 evaluates every series iteration for every element, so the fast E₁ shown above becomes essential.
Compilation adds several seconds per model (see the setup column above).

For many spectra at once: this is where a GPU wins.

Batching many leaves. Running thousands of leaves (and chains) side by side with jax.vmap, e.g. all 340 ANGERS and LOPEX leaves, gives millions of band evaluations per step. That keeps a GPU busy, so the cost per leaf could drop by one to two orders of magnitude.
The better error models are GPU-shaped. The GP discrepancy and the library-learned discrepancy recommended on Error models are mostly matrix products and low-rank updates. The hierarchical library model is one large model over many spectra.

Recommendation.

Single-leaf fits: stay on the CPU with the fast E₁ and nutpie or NumPyro, and consider fitting at a coarser wavelength step. Cost scales directly with the number of bands, and the residuals are correlated over tens of nm.
Library-scale or hierarchical models: move to JAX on a GPU, with the fast E₁.

title: Bayesian PROSPECT-D inversion in five probabilistic programming toolchains
text:
Main findings

The toolchains recover the same posterior. On every spectrum and parameter, posterior medians agree within Monte Carlo error (max R̂ = 1.009), and on the synthetic leaf all five recover the true parameters. There is one exception: BayesianTools on an03r0185 (R̂ = 1.69). One of BayesianTools’ four DEzs runs got stuck, all 3 of its internal chains together, at a much worse fit (σ ≈ 0.02 vs 0.007) on the white leaf, whose pigments sit near zero. Its other 9 chains agree with the NUTS and slice samplers. Separately, BayesianTools on an03r0271 reached R̂ = 1.011 (borderline; ESS is adequate). See Backends.
Efficiency differs more than accuracy. The median worst-parameter ESS/s ranges from 5.7 to 21.0. PyMC is fastest, then BayesianTools; Stan, Turing and NIMBLE are close together. The NUTS backends slow down about 5× on the thickest, wettest leaves, where N, Cw and Cm are strongly correlated. The gradient-free samplers keep a fixed cost per iteration. Compilation and JIT time (Stan about 45 s once per model, NIMBLE about 45 s per fit, Julia about 15 s per session) matter for single-leaf workflows.
Exact vs. approximate \(E_1\) hardly matters. The Swamee–Ohija closed form changes R and T by ≲ 8×10⁻⁴ and shifts posteriors by a fraction of a posterior SD. Its τ < 0 failure (k > 11.6) does occur in strong water bands, so it needs the usual clamp at 0. See Forward model.
The iid error model is the weak link, not the sampler. Residuals are smooth, autocorrelated over tens of nm, several times the replicate noise, and shared across leaves. Under iid errors only 4/40 measured trait values fall inside the 90% intervals, and held-out transmittance coverage is 27%. A heteroskedastic AR(1) likelihood (exact, \(O(n)\)) raises these to 12/40 and 76%, and also improves held-out T RMSE (0.053 → 0.040). Its AR coefficient runs into φ → 1, though, which points to smoother GP or library-learned discrepancy models as the next step. See Error models.
PyMC can go faster without changing the model. Replacing the default sampler and Cephes \(E_1\) with nutpie + fast E₁ raises the median ESS/s from 21.0 to 29.4 (1.4×). The fast \(E_1\) (NAG Chebyshev, ≤ 2×10⁻¹² error) helps every sampler. JAX’s built-in exp1 is very slow on CPU, and Swamee–Ohija is never the fastest choice. See Faster PyMC.
A bug fix along the way. The PROSPECT-D t21 in rrtm used the wrong refractive index; fixed in ashiklom/rrtm#10.

The first-round model treats PROSPECT’s misfit as one wavelength-independent Gaussian SD with independent bands. On Traits and Spectra, that gives posteriors that are much too narrow, and held-out transmittance predictions whose 90% intervals miss most of the data. This page diagnoses why, lays out better error models, and fits one of them (heteroskedastic + AR(1)) as a demonstration.

title: Better error models
text:
What the residuals look like




                                                


Figure 1: Reflectance residuals (observed − posterior median, Stan, iid) for every real leaf (gray) and their mean across leaves (blue). Hover a gray line to identify the leaf.








                                                


Figure 2: Left: autocorrelation of the reflectance residuals vs. lag (in nm), per leaf (gray) and averaged (blue). Right: for the five LOPEX leaves, SD across the 5 replicate measurements (instrument + leaf-placement noise) vs. RMS model residual, by wavelength. Log scale.




Three things stand out:

The residuals are smooth, not noisy. The mean autocorrelation stays above 0.5 out to a lag of about 35 nm. At 1 nm sampling, 2000 bands carry the information of only a few dozen independent observations. The iid likelihood counts all 2000, so it is overconfident by roughly a factor of \(\sqrt{2000/\text{(a few dozen)}}\) in posterior SD.
The residuals are mostly model error, not measurement error. For the LOPEX leaves, the RMS residual is a median of about 0× the replicate-to-replicate SD. Instrument noise is a small part of the misfit.
The residuals share structure across leaves. The mean residual has features at the same wavelengths in very different leaves: the blue end below ~450 nm, the green peak and red edge, and the 1450/1940 nm water bands. These are PROSPECT-D’s structural errors, and they can be learned.

A good error model therefore needs (i) a wavelength-dependent scale, (ii) correlation between neighboring bands, and ideally (iii) a systematic component shared across leaves, kept separate from (iv) a small instrument-noise term.

title: Better error models
text:
Candidate error models
Write the observation as \(y(\lambda) = R(\lambda;\theta) + \delta(\lambda) + \varepsilon(\lambda)\): \(\delta\) is structured model discrepancy and \(\varepsilon\) is measurement noise. The options below run roughly from cheapest to most complete. All of them fit in any of the five backends; cost is per log-density evaluation, with \(n\approx 2000\) bands.











Model
What it captures
Cost
Notes




A
Heteroskedastic scale: \(\sigma(\lambda) = \sigma_0 + \sigma_1 R(\lambda)\), or \(\log\sigma(\lambda) = \sum_k \beta_k B_k(\lambda)\) (B-spline, random-walk prior on \(\beta\))
Wavelength-dependent magnitude
\(O(n)\)
The spline form is weakly identified from one spectrum; learn \(\beta\) across many leaves (C, E).


B
AR(1) / Ornstein–Uhlenbeck correlation: \(z_i = \phi z_{i-1} + \sqrt{1-\phi^2}\,\eta_i\), with \(\varepsilon_i = \sigma_i z_i\)
Band-to-band autocorrelation
\(O(n)\), exact (tridiagonal precision, \(\log\lvert\Sigma\rvert = (n-1)\log(1-\phi^2)\))
For uneven spacing use \(\phi_i = e^{-\Delta\lambda_i/\ell}\) (exponential/Matérn-½ kernel). Demonstrated below (A + B).


B′
Smoother stationary processes (Matérn-3/2, 5/2) in state-space form
Smooth residuals without AR(1)’s rough small-lag behavior
\(O(n)\) via Kalman filter
Same idea as B with a better-matched smoothness. Needs a Kalman-filter log-likelihood in each DSL.


C
Hierarchical, wavelength-specific variance shared across a library: \(\log\sigma_\ell(\lambda) = \mu_\sigma(\lambda) + u_\ell\)
Which bands PROSPECT fits poorly, learned from data
\(O(n)\) per leaf
Pool across leaves (and instruments) so a per-band \(\sigma\) becomes identifiable.


D
Gaussian-process discrepancy (Kennedy & O’Hagan 2001): \(\delta \sim \mathcal{GP}(0, k_\psi)\), \(\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_\text{inst}^2(\lambda))\)
Smooth systematic misfit separated from noise
\(O(nm)\) with a Hilbert-space low-rank GP (\(m\approx 30\)–\(60\) basis functions); \(O(n)\) for Markov kernels
Allows nonstationarity (separate length-scales for VIS / NIR / SWIR, or input warping). \(\delta\) competes with \(\theta\), so its amplitude needs an informative prior, ideally from E. Fix \(\sigma_\text{inst}\) from replicates.


E
Empirical-Bayes discrepancy from a spectral library: \(\delta \sim \mathcal N(\mu(\lambda), \Lambda\Lambda^\top + D)\) with \(k\approx 5\)–\(10\) factors
Recurring structural error (mean bias and its main modes)
\(O(nk^2)\) via Woodbury
Fit \(\mu\), \(\Lambda\), \(D\) by inverting many leaves (e.g. all 276 ANGERS + 64 LOPEX) hierarchically, or by PCA of residuals as a quick first pass. Instrument-specific \(\mu\) absorbs sphere-vs-clip differences.


F
Heavy tails: Student-\(t\) marginals or a \(t\)-process
Outliers, detector-splice steps (ASD at 1000/1800 nm), specular artifacts
\(O(n)\)
Combine with B/D for robustness.


G
Likelihood tempering by effective sample size, \(\ell(\theta)\cdot n_\text{eff}/n\) (as in PEcAnRTM::neff)
Overconfidence only
\(O(n)\)
A quick patch: it widens posteriors but does not model the shape of the misfit or make predictive bands right. A baseline, not a solution.



Recommendation. Use E + B/D as the target model, with the A + B model below as the cheap default:

Invert a large library (ANGERS + LOPEX + others) hierarchically and learn the discrepancy mean \(\mu(\lambda)\) and a low-rank covariance \(\Lambda\). Learn per-instrument noise \(D\) from replicates.
For individual leaves, use the learned \(\mu\) and \(\Lambda\Lambda^\top + D\) as a fixed, informative discrepancy model. Add a leaf-specific AR(1)/Matérn term with a small amplitude for whatever the factors miss.
Validate with the checks already on this site: coverage of measured traits, and coverage of held-out transmittance. Where T exists, fitting R and T jointly with correlated R/T discrepancies is the other big win.

Demonstration: heteroskedastic + AR(1) (Stan)

Takeaways.

The estimated band-to-band correlation is very high (median \(\phi \approx\) 0.999), which confirms that the residual is a smooth process. In effect, the AR(1) model judges the spectrum to carry far less independent information than the iid model assumes.
For most leaves \(\phi\) is pushed against its upper bound of 1. There the stationary AR(1) is degenerating towards a random walk: the residual is smoother than any stationary AR(1) process can represent. That is direct evidence for the smoother Matérn / state-space or GP discrepancy models (B′, D). It also makes sampling harder: NUTS needs step sizes of about 0.02 and trees of depth 7–8 near the boundary.
Trait intervals widen a lot, and coverage of the measured traits improves accordingly. The posterior medians move too, because the AR(1) likelihood weights smooth, broad features over individual bands.
It predicts the held-out transmittance better, not just more cautiously: both T RMSE and T coverage improve (table above). The in-sample reflectance RMSE gets worse, because the model no longer chases every band. That is the right trade-off, since the iid fit was over-fitting structured residuals.
Each log-density evaluation costs about the same as iid (the extra work is \(O(n)\) arithmetic), but the posterior geometry is harder: median Stan sampling time is 2307 s vs. 363 s for iid, mostly from the deeper NUTS trees near \(\phi \to 1\).
What AR(1) does not fix: the discrepancy has structure that is shared across leaves (the blue mean residual above), which a stationary zero-mean process cannot represent. That is the motivation for models D and E above. The held-out transmittance check is the natural test of whether they work.
